1. Definitions and Lemmas

In this section we establish notation and recall basic definitions from sheaf theory that will be used throughout the paper. Our conventions follow standard references, with one exception noted below in Remark 1.2. The reader familiar with this material may safely skip to the next section.

Definition 1.1.

A sheaf on a topological space X is a functor satisfying the gluing axiom and the locality axiom.

Remark 1.2.

Note that presheaves do not satisfy the gluing axiom in general.

Lemma 1.3 (Key Lemma).

Every injective sheaf is flasque.

Proof.

Let F be an injective sheaf. We show every restriction map is surjective. Consider any open inclusion U subset V. By injectivity of F, the map Hom(j_! Z_U, F) to Hom(Z_V, F) is surjective. This gives the claim.

Corollary 1.4.

Injective resolutions of sheaves always exist.

Example 1.5.

The constant sheaf Z on a manifold is a canonical example.

In this section we develop the foundations of sheaf theory required for the main results. The reader familiar with Grothendieck's six operations may skip ahead to Section 2 where we apply these tools.

2. Main Theorem

Theorem 2.1 (Main Theorem).

Under the hypotheses of the previous section, the derived pushforward commutes with flat base change.

Remark 2.2.

The base change condition is necessary as shown by a counterexample.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

We use the flat base change theorem. The key steps are: (1) reduce to the affine case, (2) apply the Kunneth formula, (3) use cohomology and base change.
